in itself due to its connection to felicity and human fiourishing, as stated in: I did not create the jinn and the humans except that they may worship M e (51:56).

… and the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: ‘I will surely fill hell with jinn and humans, all together!’This means that God’s decree has been realized and His promise has been validated by those who wronged themselves and disagreed about the truth after knowledge came to them out of enmity among themselves. And the term ‘word’ (kalima) here refers to: ‘I will surely fill hell …’

This verse is similar in meaning to: Had We wished We would have given every soul its guidance, but M y word became due: ‘Surely I will fill hell with all the jinn and humans.’ (32:13). The origin of this statement is what God Almighty said to Iblis, the Accursed, when he stated: ‘By Your might, I will surely pervert them, except Your exclusive servants among them.’ He said, ‘The truth is that—and I speak the truth—I will surely fill hell with you and all of those who follow you’ (38:85). These verses are consistent in their content and clarify one other’s meaning.

Reflecting on the meanings of these verses, we can derive the following conclusions:

Firstly, when God says, Had your Lord wished, He would have made mankind one community, it means uniting them by eliminating differences and disagreements among them. Some say it refers to compelling everyone to submit and removing free will. However, this would have contradicted the principle of moral accountability (taklīf), and hence God did not do it. Some attribute this view to Qatāda. Others say the meaning is that if He willed, He could have gathered everyone together in Paradise, but He wanted to reward you for your deeds, a viewpoint attributed to Abū Muslim. It is evident, based on their context, that the present verses do not support either interpretation.

Secondly, when He says, … but they continue to differ, He means they will persistently disagree concerning the religion, implying a departure from the truth, which is then masked and depicted in various false images resembling the truth. Some interpret this to mean differences in livelihoods and conditions, essentially differences that are non-religious, a viewpoint attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. However, the reader will be well aware from our previous discussions that this does not match the context of the preceding verses. Others argue that ‘differ’ here implies that some follow their predecessors blindly and engage in the same falsehoods as they did, an explanation that, like the previous one, is at odds with the context of the verses. This is further elucidated in the verse, Certainly W e gave M oses the Book, but differences arose about it … (3:93).

Thirdly, the statement, except those on whom your Lord has mercy is a reference to those whom God has guided among the believers.

Fourthly, the demonstrative pronoun ‘that’ in the phrase, and that is why He created them, refers to mercy, which is the ultimate goal God intended for His creation, so they might find true happiness and felicity. Some have argued that the intended meaning is that God created humankind for discord and disagreement, attributing this opinion to al-Ḥasan

al-Baṣrī and ʿAtāʾ. However, the reader will note that this reading is rather superficial and weak. Yes, if the pronoun ‘them’ in ‘He created them’ is taken to refer to the rest of humankind after the exception of those on whom your Lord has mercy, then, considering discord as a purpose of the remainder’s creation would be plausible. This would make the verse somewhat parallel in meaning to His statement, Certainly We have created for hell many of the jinn and humans (7:179).

Others have argued that the demonstrative pronoun refers to the entirety of what the discourse indicates about God’s will in creating them, namely that they are predisposed to disagreements and divisions in their knowledge, perceptions, opinions, feelings, and everything that follows, such as their will and choices in practice. This includes matters of religion, faith, obedience, and disobedience. In essence, the primary objective is disagreement and difference in general, whether it is religious or otherwise. This view has been attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās based on what has been narrated from him, namely that he said: ‘God created them as two groups: One group He has mercy upon and they do not differ, and another group He does not have mercy upon and they do differ.’ Malik b. Anas is reported to have said concerning the meaning of the verse: ‘God created them so that there would be a group in paradise and a group in hellfire.’ However, the foolishness of such explanations should be plain to the discerning reader. Therefore, we will not waste time by dwelling on them further.

Fifthly, the meaning of and the word of your Lord has been fulfilled refers to its realization and its actualization in objective reality.

Examining Narrations

(1) In Tafsīr al-Qummī, regarding the verse, Your Lord will indeed recompense everyone fully for their works (11:111), it is said that Imām ʿAlī commented, ‘It pertains to the Day of Resurrection.’

(2) In al-Durr al-manthūr, both Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrate from al-Ḥasan, who narrated regarding the verse, So go aright, just as you have been commanded—and whoever has turned with you (11:112): ‘W hen this verse was revealed, he exclaimed, ‘Be firm! Be firm!’ and from then on, he was never seen to laugh.’

(3) In Majmaʿ al-bayān, regarding the verse, So go aright, just as you have been commanded: Ibn ʿAbbās remarked, ‘No verse was revealed to the Prophet that was harder or more demanding on him than this one. This is why, when his companions noted, “Your hair has turned grey so quickly, O Messenger of God,” he responded, “The chapters Hūd and al-Wāqiʿa have turned my hair grey!”

Author’s comment: The well-known phrasing of the tradition is, ‘Hūd and its sisters have turned my hair grey’, though the lack of content in al-W āqiʿa that mirrors the verse, So go aright, just as you have been commanded, suggests it may not have been this verse being specifically referred

to in the narration. The theme common to both chapters is their discourse about the Day of Resurrection.

(4) In Tafsīr al-Qummī, about the verse, And do not incline toward the wrongdoers (11:113), it is said that Imām ʿAlī commented: ‘To incline means to show them afiection, give them sincere advice, and to obey them.”

Author’s comment: This tradition is also narrated M ajmaʿ al-bayān, with a disconnected chain from the Infallibles .

(5) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from ʿUthmān b. ʿĪsā, from a man, from Imām al-Ṣādiq about the verse, And do not incline toward the wrongdoers, lest the Fire should touch you, He said:

‘Indeed, He did not make it an eternal punishment for them, but a deterrent lest the Fire should touch you, so do not incline towards them.’

Author’s comment: Instead of saying ‘the Fire will seize you’, He said it will ‘touch you’, making it a brief touch.

(6) In the same source, it is narrated from Jarīr from Imām al-Ṣādiq , about the verse, Maintain the prayer at the two ends of the day

(11:114):‘The two ends refer to dusk and dawn, and during the early hours of the night pertains to the final evening prayer (ʿishāʾ).’ (7) In Tahdhīb al-Ahkām, Shaykh al-Ṭūsī narrates via a chain of narrators from Zurāra from Imām al-Bāqir , discussing the five daily

prayers, God’s statement, Maintain the prayer at the two ends of the day, and during the early hours of the night: ‘it is the final evening prayer.’

Author’s comment: I would note that the tradition clearly suggests the explanation of the two ends of the day as the period before noon and after, encompassing the five daily prayer times.

(8) In M aʿānī al-Akhbār, al-Ṣadūq transmits via his chain of narration from Ibrāhīm b. ʿUmar, who heard from someone, who reported from Imām al-Ṣādiq regarding the words of God Almighty, Indeed good deeds efface misdeeds: ‘The believer’s night prayer (salāt al-muʾmin bi al-layl) erases the sins committed during the day.’

Author’s comment: This tradition is also narrated in al-Kāfī, Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, the Amālī of Shaykh al-Mufīd, and the Amālī of Shaykh al-Ṭūsī.

(9) In M ajmaʿ al-bayān, al-Ṭabrisī narrates from al-Wāḥidī, with a chain of transmitters going back to Ḥammād b. Salama, who heard from ʿAlī b. Zayd, who reported from Abū ʿUthmān, who said: ‘I was with Salmān under a tree when he took a dry twig from it and shook it until its leaves fell of . He then said, “O Abū ʿUthmān, won’t you ask me why I did that?” I said, “Why did you do that?” He replied, “The Messenger of God , did the same when I was with him under a tree. He took a dry twig, shook it until its leaves fell of , and then asked, “Won’t you ask me, O Salmān, why I did this?” I asked, “Why did you do it?” He said, “When a Muslim performs ablution properly and then prays the five daily prayers, his sins fall from him just as these leaves fell from the twig.” He then recited this verse M aintain the prayer… to the end of it.’

Author’s comment: This narration is also quoted in al-Durr al-manthūr, narrated by al-Ṭayālīsī, Aḥmad, al-Dāramī, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Baghawī in his Muʿjam, and Ibn Mardawayh, without a complete chain.

(10) In Majmaʿ al-bayān, with a chain going back to al-Ḥārith, it is reported from ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib who said: ‘We were with the Messenger of God in the mosque waiting for the prayer when a man stood up and said, “O Messenger of God, I have committed a sin.” The Prophet ignored him. But after the Prophet completed the prayer, the man repeated his statement. The Prophet said, “Didn’t you just pray with us and perform a proper ablution?”

The man replied, “Yes.” The Prophet said, “That prayer has atoned for your sin.”’

Author’s comment: This narration is transmitted through many chains from Ibn Masʿūd, Abī Umāma, Muʿādh b. Jabal, Ibn ʿAbbās, Burayda, Wāthila b. al-Asqaʿ, Anas, and others, although the precise details of the story differ from one person to another. It is narrated by al-Tirmidhī and others from Abū al-Yusr, who is the main person in the story.

(11) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from Abū Hamza al-Thumālī that he said: ‘I heard one of the two of them , say that ʿAlī once asked the people, “Which verse in the Book of God is the most hopeful in your eyes?” Some of them replied, Indeed Allah does not forgive that any partner should be ascribed to Him, but He forgives anything besides that to whomever He wishes. He said, “It is good, but it is not the one I had in mind.” Others said, ‘O My servants who have committed excesses against their own souls, do not despair of the mercy of Allah …’ He said, “It is good, but it is not the one I had in mind.” Yet others mentioned, and those who, when they commit an indecent act or wrong themselves, remember Allah, and plead for forgiveness for their sins. He said, “It is good, but it is not the one I had in mind.”’

The narrator continued: ‘Then the people fell silent. He asked, “What is the matter with you, O assembly of Muslims?” They responded,”’By God, we have nothing else.” He replied, “I heard the Messenger of God say: The most hopeful verse in the Book of God is: Maintain the prayer at the two ends of the day, and during the early hours of the night. He recited the whole verse and said, ‘O ʿAlī, by He who sent me with the truth as a giver of glad tidings and a warner—when one of you goes for his ablution, sins fall from his limbs. When he turns his face and his heart to the prayer, he is as free from sins as he was when his mother gave birth to him.

If something occurs between the prayers, it is the same until the five prayers are completed.’

He continued, ‘O ʿAlī, the status of the five daily prayers for my community is like a flowing river at the doorstep of one of you. What would you think if a person had dirt on his body and bathed in that river five times a day? Would there be any dirt left on him? Similar to this, by God, are the five daily prayers are for my community!’”’

Author’s comment: The analogy mentioned at the end of the narration has been reported through various Sunnī sources from several companions, including Abū Hurarra, Anas, Jābir, and Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī

from him .

(12) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from Ibrāhīm al-Karkhī: ‘I was with Abū ʿAbd Allāh (al-Ṣādiq) when a man from the people of Medina entered. Abū ʿAbd Allāh asked him, Where have you come from?’ The man did not answer, so Abū ʿAbd Allāh said, ‘You have come from here and there. Reflect on what you do in your day. An angel is assigned to you, recording what you do. Do not belittle a sin even if it seems small, for one day it will harm you. Also, do not belittle a good deed; nothing is more eagerly sought after than a good deed. It reaches even the oldest and greatest of sins, erasing them, and making them fall away and leaving you free from them. This is God’s statement, Indeed good deeds efface misdeeds. That is an admonition for the mindful.’

(13) In the same source, it is narrated from Sumāʿa b. M ihrān: ‘A man from the people of Jibāl (Western Iran) asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh about someone who acquired wealth through working for the ruler. He donates from it, maintains ties of kinship, and goes on pilgrimage hoping to be forgiven for what he earned, quoting the verse, Indeed good deeds efface misdeeds. Abū ʿAbd Allāh replied, “A sin does not atone for a sin. But a good deed can atone for a sin.”

Then Abū ʿAbd Allāh said, “If lawful and forbidden are mixed together, becoming indistinguishable, and one cannot differentiate between the lawful and the forbidden, then there is no problem.”’

(14) In al-Durr al-manthūr, al-Suyūṭī reports from Aḥmad and al-Ṭabarānī, who transmit from Abū Umāma who said, ‘The Messenger of God , stated: “There is no Muslim man who has a prescribed prayer to perform and stands to perform ablution, perfecting it, and then prays, perfecting his prayer, except that God forgives his sins between that prayer and the previous one.”’

Author’s comment: Narrations on this topic are numerous. Whoever wishes to carry out a detailed examination should refer to the compilations of traditions.

(15) In al-Durr al-manthūr, it is narrated from al-Ṭabarānī, Abū alShaykh, Ibn M ardawayh, al-Daylamī, from Jarīr that: ‘I heard the Messenger of God being asked about the explanation of this verse:

Your Lord would never destroy the townships unjustly while their inhabitants were bringing about reform (11:117). The Messenger of God responded: “It means their people treated each other fairly.”’ (16) In al-Kāfī, it is transmitted from ʿAbd Allāh b. Sinān, who asked Imām al-Ṣādiq , about the verse: Had your Lord wished, He would have made mankind one community; but they continue to differ, except those on whom your Lord has mercy (11:118–119). He replied: “They were one community, and then God sent prophets to establish a conclusive proofs for them.”’

Author’s comment: A similar narration has been cited by al-Ṣadūq in Maʿānī al-Akhbār.

(17) In Maʿānī al-Akhbār, Shaykh al-Ṣadūq transmits via his chain of narrators from Abū Baṣīr, that he asked Imām al-Ṣādiq about the verse, I did not create the jinn and the humans except that they may worship M e (51:56). He said: ‘God created them to command them to worship.’ And he asked about the verse, but they continue to differ, except those on whom your Lord has mercy—and that is why He created them (11:118–119). He said: ‘He created them to perform acts that make them deserving of His mercy, so He may have mercy on them.’

(18) In Tafsīr al-Qummī, it is narrated from Abū al-Jārūd, from Abū Jaʿfar : ‘But they continue to differ, except those on whom your Lord has mercy—it refers to the family of Muḥammad and their followers. And as for the verse, and that is why He created them, it means that the people of mercy do not differ about religion.’

(19) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from Yaʿqūb b. Saʿīd, from Imām al-Ṣādiq , about the verse, I did not create the jinn and the humans except that they may worship M e (51:56). He replied: ‘God created them for worship.’ And about the verse, but they continue to differ, except those on whom your Lord has mercy—and that is why He created them, he said: ‘This verse was revealed after the former one.’

Author’s comment: This points to the notion that the second verse, which says except those on whom your Lord has mercy—and that is why He created them, serves as a specific verse that abrogates the general meaning of the previous verse. It has been previously discussed in our treatment of abrogation that, according to the teachings of the Prophet’s Household , the concept of abrogation is broader than what is conventionally understood by scholars of Islamic legal theory. The specific verses, in their formative essence, overrule the meaning of the general verses, as specific contexts

and factors have a more direct effect than general stipulations. Understand this well.
